subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Pooja, you asked how I did it. Honestly, I was terrified. It's Ayesha, remember. At the bus-stop shelter an older guy kept crowding a girl who was gripping her bag, and everyone was looking at their phones. I did not shout. I walked up and said, "Hey, there you are!" as if I knew her, and asked her to sit with me. She did, fast. The guy hovered a bit, then wandered off when I stared at the timetable really hard. When the bus came I told the conductor to keep an eye out for her stop. Small stuff. But I keep thinking, I did not have to fight anyone.

qa.q: What did Ayesha say to the girl at the bus stop?
qa.a: Ayesha said, "Hey, there you are!" as if they already knew each other, and asked her to sit down.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when walking up to the girl?
qa.a: Ayesha was terrified but chose a low-risk action; the words "honestly, I was terrified" show the fear was real even though the action was small.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha's approach work without a confrontation?
qa.a: Ayesha gave the girl a way out and a companion, and asked the conductor to look out for her stop, small safe steps rather than an all-or-nothing act of heroism.

qa.q: What might the girl have felt when Ayesha said "Hey, there you are!" and offered a seat?
qa.a: The girl probably felt relief and safety; sitting fast suggests she was glad someone had noticed and given her an easy way to leave the situation.

grounding: A teenager chooses a low-risk action such as checking on the target and distracting the aggressor, showing safe helping is a range of options.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: I was on the metro platform watching everything, and here is what I saw. A man had grabbed a boy's phone out of a group of schoolkids and was jeering at them. Six or seven commuters stood around. Jahnavi, a girl in a college lanyard, did not shout. She walked up to the boy, asked, "Are you okay? Do you want to call someone?" and stood next to him. Deepika, another passenger, quietly pressed the help button at the pillar and spoke to the station staff. The man saw the two of them and the staff coming and dropped the phone. Jahnavi stayed beside the boy until the guard arrived.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi ask the boy?
qa.a: Jahnavi asked, "Are you okay? Do you want to call someone?"

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi have chosen to stand next to the boy instead of shouting?
qa.a: Jahnavi seems to want to help calmly and safely, showing care for the boy first; standing beside him signals support without provoking the man.

qa.q: What small action by Deepika made a difference?
qa.a: Deepika pressed the help button and told the station staff, a low-risk action that brought adults in without any confrontation.

qa.q: What might the boy have been feeling before and after Jahnavi stood beside him?
qa.a: The boy was probably scared and embarrassed before, and relieved afterwards that someone checked on him and stayed until the guard arrived.

grounding: A teenager and another passenger choose low-risk actions, checking on the target and calling for help, seen by a bystander.
